description: We’re a collaborative team passionate about space, technology, and creative problem-solving. We’re building an engaging project using NASA data and combining technical and creative skills. We’re looking for active teammates with skills in backend, AI/ML, data analysis, graphic design, astronomy, or data visualization.
summary: LUNIX is an interactive, browser-based tool designed for lunar exploration. Developed as a comprehensive solution, it allows users to evaluate and compare potential lunar landing sites, allowing for both predefined sites (such as Artemis or historical Apollo sites) and user-chosen coordinates. LUNIX features a dynamic polar skyplot that visualises the paths of the Sun and Earth relative to local lunar terrain constraints. Users can control time, simulate launch delays, and assess critical mission telemetry through a 30-day forecast ribbon. This includes monitoring solar array power-generation efficiency and tracking Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication blackout windows. Featuring two user personas (Engineer and Explorer) and a split-screen comparative scorecard, LUNIX makes complex lunar data accessible while integrating directly with NASA's JPL Horizons and ASU's LROC QuickMap for extended verification. It serves as a link between user-friendly, enthusiast tools, high-precision expert tools, and modern speed requirements.
details:
Core Functionality and Operation

The Lunar Site Navigator is an interactive, client-side web application designed to simulate and visualize critical environmental conditions at various lunar landing sites. It operates by calculating the precise ephemeris (positions) of the Sun and Earth relative to specific lunar coordinates and times, utilizing Julian day conversions and orbital mechanics mathematics. Users can select from predefined historic and proposed sites (such as Apollo 11, Shackleton Rim, or Chang'e 4) or input custom latitude and longitude coordinates. The application dynamically renders an overhead polar skyplot and an interactive 30-day forecast ribbon to display real-time solar elevations, terrain shadowing, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility.

Key Benefits and Intended Impact

This tool benefits mission planners, space enthusiasts, and educators by translating complex astronomical data into a highly accessible, visual format. The intended impact is to enable rapid, high-level feasibility assessments for lunar surface operations. By immediately demonstrating when a site will fall into lunar night or lose direct radio contact with Earth, the application highlights strict survival and operational constraints for uncrewed landers and rovers. It successfully bridges the gap between raw mathematical data and general comprehension by offering two distinct user personas: an "Engineer" mode that outputs precise telemetry and an "Explorer" mode that provides plain-English summaries of the environmental conditions.

Technology Stack and Development Tools

The application was built entirely as a standalone, single-file frontend web project without the need for a backend server.

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and modern vanilla JavaScript.
  • Frameworks: Tailwind CSS (implemented via CDN) was utilized for rapid, responsive UI styling and layout structuring.
  • Rendering: The native HTML5 Canvas API is used to draw the dynamic polar skyplots, celestial body trajectories, and the interactive timeline ribbons.
  • Typography: Google Fonts (Inter and JetBrains Mono) were integrated for a clean, technical aesthetic.
  • External Integration: The application dynamically generates verification links to external NASA tools, specifically ASU's LROC QuickMap and the JPL Horizons API.

Creativity and Unique Features

The project demonstrates creativity by replacing the dense, intimidating spreadsheets typically associated with orbital mechanics with a sleek, dark-themed dashboard. It features a custom-built, lightweight CSS tooltip engine and interactive sliders that allow users to scrub through time or simulate launch delays ("slips") of up to 14 days, updating the UI instantly. Furthermore, a split-screen "Compare Sites" feature generates a head-to-head scorecard, allowing users to evaluate and contrast the maximum continuous sunlight, peak solar elevation, and comms blackout periods of two distinct locations simultaneously.

Design and Engineering Factors Considered

During development, the team had to account for the unique topography of the Moon, particularly at the Artemis target regions near the poles. To address this without requiring massive topographical datasets, a procedural horizon generator was implemented to simulate synthetic terrain masks (mare, crater, rim, or peak) based on the site's latitude. The team also considered the physical hardware limitations of lunar landers by building in a solar array efficiency calculator. This feature adjusts the projected power yield based on whether the panels are flat, vertical, or tracking—a critical consideration given the low, grazing angles of sunlight at the lunar south pole.
